claims.statement: Marcus Aurelius was born at Rome, in a villa on the Caelian Hill, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May (26 April in the Julian calendar) in 121 CE.
He was educated in rhetoric by Fronto, was adopted by the emperor Antoninus Pius in 138 CE, became emperor in 161 CE, at first jointly with Lucius Verus, and ruled alone from 169 CE.

Much of his reign was spent on campaign in central Europe, and the Meditations were probably written there, about 171 to 175 CE; the first book ends 'Among the Quadi at the Granua' and the second 'This in Carnuntum'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the index visit on the Danube frontier; the sources do not fix where he was on the true-frame index date.

claims.statement: A great pestilence struck the empire during his reign, from 165 CE, spread with the Parthian war and the wars on the Danube; the Life of Marcus says the dead were removed in carts and wagons and that thousands died, many nobles among them. Galen witnessed the epidemic.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; the modern sick visit is not a claim about this epidemic.

claims.statement: The cause of the Antonine Plague is uncertain: Galen's case reports suggest smallpox to many authors, but paleopathological confirmation is lacking.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective identification of the epidemic; not coded.

claims.statement: Cassius Dio, a senator of the period, writes that he was so frail in body that at first he could not endure the cold, that he ate very little and only at night, and that by day he took nothing but the drug called theriac, 'not so much because he feared anything, as because his stomach and chest were in bad condition'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the presenting problem: chronic stomach and chest complaints. No diagnosis can be made from the description.

claims.statement: In a speech that Dio gives him, addressed to his soldiers after hearing of the revolt of Avidius Cassius, he describes himself as already an old man and weak, 'unable to take either food without pain or sleep without anxiety'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Speeches in ancient histories were composed by the historian; the words are Dio's, but they fit his other descriptions. After the index date, so not linked to the modern episode.

claims.statement: In the Meditations he thanks the gods that remedies were shown to him in dreams, among them remedies 'against bloodspitting and giddiness', and that his body had held out so long in such a kind of life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own words; the cause of the blood-spitting and giddiness is unknown and is not diagnosed.

claims.statement: Galen became court physician to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, and prepared his theriac at the court; Marcus Aurelius took theriac daily, to protect against poisons and for his general health.
Theriac was a compound remedy of many ingredients, among them viper's flesh, opium, honey, wine and cinnamon.
Galen relates that the emperor disliked the drowsiness the theriac caused, so the poppy juice was left out; he then could not sleep, and the opium-containing preparation was resumed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Read only in a magazine summary of Galen's account (On Antidotes); no scholarly translation was read. Anchors the modern dependence assessment, which is not a claim about him.

claims.statement: Whether he was dependent on or addicted to opium is disputed. Thomas Africa argued for addiction in 1961; later reviews find no explicit ancient description of opium dependence, call his the one putative case, and favour the most parsimonious reading, that the opium was medicinal rather than hedonic.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Disputed retrospective claim; no opioid use disorder is attributed to him and none is coded.

claims.statement: He died on 17 March (Julian) 180 CE, on campaign, at 58; Dio gives his age as fifty-eight years, ten months and twenty-two days. The Life of Marcus says that, eager to die, he refrained from food and drink, worsening the disease, sent his son away for fear he would catch it, and died on the seventh day. Tertullian places his death at Sirmium and Aurelius Victor at Vindobona (Vienna).
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only. The place of death is unresolved.

source_links.locator: Life of Marcus Aurelius 28 and editor's note 184

claims.statement: The cause of his death is unknown. Dio reports being told that the physicians hastened it to please Commodus; the Life of Marcus suggests a contagious illness, and its editor notes that the plague theory is not well supported.
As a boy he studied so hard that it impaired his health, which the Life of Marcus calls the only fault to be found in his entire childhood.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate chronic epigastric and lower chest pain after meals, with poor appetite and poor sleep, in a 53-year-old man who leads a large organization through a long field assignment, as current guidance advises: exclude a cardiac cause first (an ECG, a structured estimate of the chance of coronary disease, no troponin for chronic pain without an acute episode, and CT coronary angiography chosen by risk); then upper endoscopy with gastric biopsies for Helicobacter pylori, because chest pain without heartburn after a cardiac evaluation calls for objective testing for reflux; reach a diagnosis of erosive reflux esophagitis and say why peptic ulcer and functional dyspepsia were set aside; treat with an eight-week course of a proton pump inhibitor, timed meals and head-of-bed elevation, then step down to on-demand use; review, with respect and without judgment, an unregulated opium-containing herbal remedy he has taken for years (a DSM-5-TR assessment, a drug-monitoring check, a urine drug test with consent, naloxone, no sedatives or alcohol with it, and no forced taper, as the CDC 2022 guideline advises), and recognize how opioids slow the gut; treat chronic insomnia with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia rather than hypnotics; and attend to the strain of command. The modern episode is a teaching case, not a claim about the cause of his real complaints, and it does not attribute opioid addiction to him.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Aurelius returns one week after his first visit. He had CT coronary angiography early this morning and an upper endoscopy afterwards with Dr. Brandt-Oyelaran of gastroenterology, and has recovered from the sedation. Over the week the burning in his upper abdomen and lower chest has continued after his late evening meal, waking him twice with a sour taste; calcium carbonate eases it within minutes. He has had no pain on exertion, no breathlessness and no fainting. He collected the naloxone spray and keeps it by his bed. referral.urgency: Routine but prompt, within one week. He is stable, with no bleeding, difficulty swallowing or vomiting. No acid-suppressing drug has been started before the endoscopy; he has calcium carbonate as needed. He has been told to call 911 for chest pain at rest lasting more than a few minutes, or with breathlessness, sweating or fainting
referral.pertinent_history: Burning and pressing pain behind the lower sternum and in the epigastrium about half an hour after meals, mostly after one large late meal, with a sour taste and night waking; never brought on by riding or walking. Poor appetite and a 3 kg weight loss over six months. No NSAIDs or aspirin. Never smoked; wine two or three times a week (AUDIT-C 3). For about six years he has taken an unregulated compounded herbal paste containing opium, about 0.5 g at bedtime most nights, for stomach pain and sleep; prescription drug monitoring shows no controlled prescriptions; a urine drug test today, with his consent, showed morphine and codeine only, consistent with opium, with fentanyl and other drugs negative. He meets one DSM-5-TR criterion (restlessness and poor sleep when he stopped it); no opioid use disorder. Hard stools every two or three days. Chronic insomnia (Insomnia Severity Index 17). PHQ-9 8 with item 9 scored 0; GAD-7 6. Today: weight 63.0 kg (BMI 21.3), blood pressure 124/78, pulse 76; mild epigastric tenderness. ECG normal. Hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; liver tests and lipase normal; A1c 5.4%; LDL 133 mg/dL; lipoprotein(a) 38 nmol/L. No known allergy
questions: Is there an esophageal, gastric or duodenal cause for his pain after meals: reflux esophagitis, peptic ulcer, or functional dyspepsia?
Does he have Helicobacter pylori infection?
What treatment do you advise, and for how long?
Could the opium in his remedy be contributing, through slowed stomach emptying or esophageal dysmotility, and does he need manometry or emptying studies?
Does he need repeat endoscopy or other follow-up?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Aurelius, a 53-year-old man who leads a large organization on a long field assignment, is seen at the request of Dr. Ashworth-Nnamdi one week after his first visit. For more than a year he has had burning and pressure behind the lower breastbone and in the upper abdomen about half an hour after eating, worst after the single large meal he eats late at night shortly before lying down, with a sour taste in the mouth and waking at night. Antacid eases it within minutes. It does not come on with exertion. He has no difficulty or pain swallowing, vomiting, black stools or blood. His appetite has been poor and he has lost about 3 kg. He takes no NSAIDs, has never smoked, and drinks wine two or three times a week. He has taken an opium-containing herbal paste at bedtime most nights for about six years; he spoke about it openly and asked that it not be judged. Hard stools every two or three days. He had CT coronary angiography this morning.
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Ashworth-Nnamdi's intake note and results: normal ECG; hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; normal liver tests and lipase; urine drug test with morphine and codeine only. CT coronary angiography this morning: coronary calcium score 0, no plaque or stenosis (CAD-RADS 0). Upper endoscopy this morning under moderate sedation: mucosal breaks longer than 5 mm in the distal esophagus, not continuous between folds (Los Angeles grade B); a 2 cm sliding hiatal hernia; no Barrett's mucosa, stricture or ring; normal stomach with no ulcer or erosion; normal duodenum. Biopsies from the antrum, incisura and body for histology and a rapid urease test, which is negative.

exam.finding: Alert after moderate sedation; pulse 74, blood pressure 122/76
Mild epigastric tenderness; no guarding, mass or enlarged liver

assessment.display: Reflux disease with erosive esophagitis, Los Angeles grade B, with a small hiatal hernia
assessment.assessment: This explains his symptoms: burning and pressure after a large meal eaten shortly before lying down, night waking with a sour taste, and relief with antacid, with coronary disease excluded this morning. There is no ulcer, so peptic ulcer disease is excluded, and functional dyspepsia is not the diagnosis when a structural cause is found. Grade B esophagitis heals in most patients with eight weeks of a proton pump inhibitor
The rapid urease test is negative off acid suppression and the stomach looks normal; histology will confirm. If it is negative, no eradication therapy is needed

Opioids slow stomach emptying and can disturb esophageal motility, and in long-term users can cause an opioid-induced esophageal dysfunction; they also cause his constipation. The esophagitis seen today is a reflux injury and should be treated in its own right. Manometry or a gastric emptying study is not needed now, since the endoscopy explains his symptoms; it would be if symptoms persisted despite healing, or if swallowing became difficult. Any change in the remedy is his decision, and is best planned with Dr. Ashworth-Nnamdi

recommendations: Omeprazole 20 mg 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast for eight weeks, then stop and use it on demand for heartburn; return to daily therapy at the lowest dose if heartburn comes back most days
Stop the calcium carbonate once omeprazole has started
The main meal at least three hours before lying down, the head of the bed raised, and little or no wine at night
Helicobacter pylori: no treatment if the histology is negative, as the rapid urease test suggests
No repeat endoscopy for grade B esophagitis while he is well; repeat endoscopy for difficulty swallowing, bleeding, weight loss or symptoms that fail to settle
High-resolution esophageal manometry and reflux monitoring off therapy only if symptoms persist despite eight weeks of treatment
No change to the remedy is needed for the esophagitis to heal; if he chooses to reduce it, a slow pace planned with his primary clinician, and polyethylene glycol for constipation meanwhile
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Ashworth-Nnamdi the same morning; she continues the prescribing and the follow-up. The endoscopy pictures were shown to Mr. Aurelius, who was relieved to hear that his heart is sound and that the problem can be treated
consultant_note.follow_up: No routine gastroenterology follow-up; Dr. Ashworth-Nnamdi will send the histology result, and he will be seen again if symptoms persist after the eight-week course or alarm features appear
